issues.legal_issue: A government must give a trustee an opportunity to be heard before extending a notification that places a religious institution under executive supervision.
material_facts: The government extended an existing notification that subjected a temple and its specific endowments to executive supervision, substantially displacing the trustees' management.
The extension decision was made without giving the trustee an opportunity to show cause.

The government had to assess whether continued supervision was required in the interests of the public good, and circumstances arising after the original notification could support cancellation or non-extension.
issues.conclusion: The extension decision was quasi-judicial, and natural justice required notice and an opportunity to be heard; because these were not provided, the notification was invalid.
issues.legal_principle: Under sections 63 and 64(1)–(3) of the Madras Hindu Religious and Charitable Endowments Act, 1951, the initial notification process included notice, objections, and an enquiry. The Court held that deciding whether to cancel or extend a notification under section 64(4) involved the same kind of assessment and had a similar effect on the trustee's rights, so natural justice also applied. Shri Radeshyam Khare v. State of Madhya Pradesh was distinguished because the statutory provisions and the nature of the orders there differed.

rule.if: notification_extension_challenge and management_rights_affected and government_assesses_need_for_continued_supervision and trustee_not_given_hearing

predicates.notification_extension_challenge: The proceeding challenges a government's decision to extend an existing notification placing a religious institution under supervision.
predicates.management_rights_affected: The notification substantially displaces or restricts the trustee's management of the institution or its endowments.
predicates.government_assesses_need_for_continued_s: The government must decide whether continued executive supervision is required in the interests of the public good.
predicates.trustee_not_given_hearing: The trustee was not given notice and an opportunity to explain why the notification should not be extended.

issues.definition: When a challenged extension affects a trustee's management, requires the government to assess the need for continued supervision, and is made without hearing the trustee, the extension is invalid.

issues.legal_issue: A natural-justice ground raised in a rejoinder and known to the respondent cannot be rejected as unraised merely because it was omitted from the original writ petition.
material_facts: The trustee did not include the natural-justice ground in the first affidavit supporting the writ petition.
The trustee expressly raised that ground in an affidavit-in-rejoinder.
The respondent had notice of the ground before the matter was argued in the High Court.
issues.conclusion: The High Court was wrong to refuse relief on the basis that the natural-justice ground had not been raised.
issues.legal_principle: A ground expressly raised in a rejoinder, where the respondent has full notice of it before argument, is properly before the court for consideration. The Court applied this principle to the writ proceedings and rejected the High Court's procedural reason for refusing relief.

predicates.writ_review_proceeding: The proceeding seeks judicial review of a government decision through a writ petition.
predicates.natural_justice_ground_in_rejoinder: The petitioner expressly raised the natural-justice objection in a rejoinder, although it was absent from the initial supporting affidavit.
predicates.respondent_received_notice: The respondent knew of the objection before the matter was argued.

issues.definition: In a writ proceeding, a natural-justice objection raised in a rejoinder and known to the respondent cannot be treated as unraised merely because it was omitted from the initial affidavit.

issues.legal_issue: A writ should not be refused as having no practical purpose on the assumption that a challenged notification will soon expire when later legislation keeps it in force.
material_facts: The High Court considered the notification likely to expire shortly after its judgment and relied on that expectation in refusing a writ.
Before the High Court delivered judgment, later legislation had come into force under which the notification would not automatically expire as the High Court assumed.
The trustee had been denied an opportunity to show cause against the notification's continuation.
issues.conclusion: The High Court's short-duration rationale was erroneous; because the notification would continue and the trustee had not been heard, the Court directed that it be quashed.
issues.legal_principle: Section 72(7) of Madras Act XXII of 1959 treated specified earlier notifications as valid under the new Act; the Court also noted that the provision was subsequently amended by Madras Act XL of 1961 with retrospective effect. Without deciding the full effect of those amendments, the Court held that the notification would not automatically expire as the High Court had assumed, and that refusing a writ on that basis was erroneous.

predicates.writ_review_proceeding: The proceeding seeks judicial review of a government notification.
predicates.challenged_notification_remains_in_force: Later legislation means the challenged notification will not automatically expire when the reviewing court assumed it would.
predicates.trustee_was_denied_hearing: The trustee was not given an opportunity to show cause against the notification's continuation.

issues.definition: When a challenged notification remains in force under later legislation and the trustee was denied a hearing, the notification should be quashed in the writ proceeding.
